what_it_does: RowHammer is a hardware attack where repeatedly reading ('hammering') a row of cells in a DRAM memory chip causes bit-flip errors in physically adjacent rows — even without touching those rows directly. Modern DDR5 memory has a built-in defense command called RFM (Refresh Management) that the memory controller issues when hammering is suspected; the DRAM chip then refreshes the vulnerable neighboring rows. The problem is that issuing an RFM command locks up the entire DRAM bank — a bank being one large partition of the chip — for 200 to 400 nanoseconds, preventing any other memory reads or writes. At very aggressive safety thresholds (triggering after fewer than 100 repeated row accesses), RFM must be issued so often that it can slow down real applications by up to 33%. AutoRFM fixes this by performing the refresh at the level of a 'subarray' — a smaller slice of the bank — rather than the whole bank, so other subarrays keep serving requests while one subarray is being refreshed. If a request arrives for the exact subarray being refreshed, the chip sends a brief signal to the memory controller asking it to retry after a short, bounded wait. To prevent attackers from deliberately targeting the same subarray repeatedly, the design also randomizes the physical mapping between memory addresses and subarrays.
